subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Discussion on the uses of pots and other things potters make (p. 137)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of clay items (pot, gullak, kulhad, birdbath) on p. 137

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the story of Mini and Appooppan from Textbook p. 137, pausing to let students look at the illustrations. Students name any clay objects they have seen or used at home.

Class discusses the first two questions from Textbook p. 137: what pots are used for, and what other kinds of things potters make. Teacher records student responses on the board under two columns — 'Uses of pots' and 'Other potter's products'.

Students share stories of clay objects in their homes or community. Teacher broadens the conversation to include gullak, kulhad, and birdbath as shown in Textbook p. 137, and prompts students to connect these to daily life occasions.

Teacher draws out the discussion with a closing question: 'Appooppan learned pottery from someone in his family — who might have taught that person?' Students share brief ideas, anchoring the idea of knowledge passing through generations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a traditional craft serves everyday needs and is passed within a community.
periods.section_context: Uses of pots, gullak, kulhad, birdbath; potter's family roles (Appooppan, Ammu, Mini); intergenerational knowledge transfer.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone in their family or neighbourhood makes things with clay. Draw out the idea that craft knowledge travels through families without labelling it — let students name the pattern themselves.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Making clay from collected soil, shaping and drying two objects (p. 138)
materials: Soil collected from a damp corner of the school compound (or damp soil brought in a container)

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly explains the day's task: students will prepare usable clay following the steps on Textbook p. 138, then shape two small objects. Students spread newspaper on desks and set out materials.

Working in small groups, students sieve the soil to remove pebbles, leaves, and plant parts, then mix the cleaned soil with a little water in the flat vessel and knead it until it holds its shape — following Textbook p. 138.

Each student uses the prepared clay to shape two small objects of their choice (a small cup, a flat tile, a pinch pot, a simple animal figure). Groups observe how wetting and kneading changed the soil's texture and made shaping possible.

Objects are placed on newspaper to begin sun-drying. Students discuss in their groups: what happened to the soil when water was added? What would happen if the clay object were baked in a kiln instead of dried in the sun?
Teacher uses the closing question from Textbook p. 137 — 'Why is the pot baked in a kiln?' — to consolidate the discussion, noting that baking makes clay hard and durable.

periods.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step material preparation process and explain how each step changes the material's properties.
periods.section_context: Soil collection, sieving, mixing with water, kneading into clay dough, shaping two objects, sun-drying; kiln baking as an alternative to drying.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let groups discover the right water-to-soil ratio by feel rather than by instruction — too wet, too dry, just right. Ask: 'How did Appooppan know when the clay was ready to shape?'

periods.textbook_anchor: A Potter's Family — Drawing products seen at a potter's place (p. 137)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of decorated clay items on p. 137

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits Mini's role in the family — she decorates pots with patterns and colours. Students look at the decorated clay items shown in Textbook p. 137 and describe the patterns they notice on the illustrated objects.

Students draw two or three potter's products they have seen or can imagine — a pot, a gullak, a kulhad, or a birdbath — and decorate them with patterns of their own invention. Students are encouraged to give each object a use in a story (a kulhad for a grandparent's morning tea, a birdbath in a garden).
Students share drawings with a partner and describe: what the object is, who might use it, and where the decoration pattern came from. Teacher circulates and asks students to name their patterns.

Brief class share-out: teacher asks two or three volunteers to hold up their drawings and explain one pattern choice. The class listens and notes any pattern that appears on something in the natural world.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of craft objects and their uses through drawing and oral explanation.
periods.section_context: Potter's products (pot, gullak, kulhad, birdbath); decorative patterns on clay items; Mini's role as decorator.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student draws a pattern they have seen on a sari, a wall, or a vessel at home, invite them to share its origin — this surfaces the living connection between domestic art and craft tradition naturally.

periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Arranging images of pot-making in correct order (p. 139)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook sequence images on p. 139 showing stages of pot-making

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 139 and look at the six images showing stages in pot-making. Teacher asks students to look carefully and not write yet — just observe what each image shows: the material, the action, the tool.

Students number the images from 1 to 6 in what they think is the correct order, working individually. Teacher moves around and asks students to explain their reasoning for placing one image before another.

Class compares answers. Where disagreement exists, teacher invites students to argue their sequence using the evidence in the images. Discussion settles the agreed order and teacher lists the stages briefly on the board.
Teacher leads a quick oral recap: students say the stages of pot-making in sequence, without looking at the textbook. This consolidates the process as a remembered narrative.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sequence the steps of a production process by reading visual evidence and explaining their reasoning.
periods.section_context: Six-stage pot-making image sequence: collecting clay, wetting and kneading, shaping on wheel, decorating, kiln firing, finished pot.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to look at what the potter's hands are doing in each image, not just the state of the pot, to reason about sequence. Pair a quieter student with a more vocal one for the comparison discussion.

periods.activity_title: Patterns on Plants — A Leaf Gallery
periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Looking around for patterns on plants and drawing a leaf pattern (p. 140)
materials: Two or three different leaves collected from the school garden or surroundings
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of leaf patterns and plant patterns on p. 140

time_bands.activity: Teacher places two or three different leaves on a shared desk at the front. Students look at them closely and describe what they see — the veins, the edges, the overall shape. Teacher asks: 'Is there a repeating element that you notice?'

Students open Textbook p. 140 and look at the illustrated leaf patterns. They then draw any one leaf pattern they can observe — from a real leaf in hand, from a plant visible through the window, or from the textbook illustration — in their notebook.

Students write one sentence beneath their drawing describing the pattern: where it repeats, what shape it makes, or which plant it comes from. They then look at the example prompt in Textbook p. 140 and add one pattern of their own choosing.

Students display their drawings to the class by holding them up. Teacher asks: 'Did anyone notice the same pattern on two different plants?' This leads into the idea that pattern shapes recur across nature.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe, draw, and describe repeating patterns found on plants in their immediate environment.
periods.section_context: Leaf vein patterns, edge patterns on leaves, neem leaf arrangement; repeating shapes observed on local plants.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to look at a real leaf at an angle to the light so veins are visible. Ask: 'Do you think a potter who decorated pots might use this pattern — why or why not?'

periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns in Nature — Drawing an animal with body patterns and a pattern on things (p. 140)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of zebra stripes, leopard spots, squirrel stripes, peacock feathers on p. 140

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 140 to the animal section and reads aloud about the zebra's stripes, the leopard's spots, the squirrel's stripes, and the peacock's feather pattern. Students identify the pattern type for each animal: stripes, spots, or another repeating shape.

Students draw one animal with its body pattern and one object from their environment that has a pattern (a checked cloth, a tiled floor, a woven mat, a printed bag). They colour both drawings to show the pattern clearly, using Textbook p. 140 as a reference.

Students write two short labels beneath their drawings: 'This animal's pattern is called ___' and 'This pattern on things looks like ___'. Pairs compare and discuss whether any animal pattern matches a pattern on an object.

Brief class discussion: teacher asks where artists might find pattern ideas. Students connect nature's patterns to Mini's decoration of pots, returning to the craft strand from the earlier part of the chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify, draw, and name repeating patterns on animals and everyday objects, connecting natural patterns to human artistic practice.
periods.section_context: Zebra stripes, leopard spots, squirrel stripes, peacock feather patterns; patterns on objects in the environment (cloth, tiles, mats).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether they have seen fabric or pottery at home that reminds them of an animal's pattern. The connection between nature and art is the key idea — let students arrive at it through their own examples.

periods.activity_title: From Mud to Brick — Same Clay, New Purpose
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Discussion on whether all houses are made of bricks and what other materials are used (p. 144)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of different house types on p. 144

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening passage about Rohan watching a building rise in Jaipur from Textbook p. 144. Students listen and then describe what they see when they pass a construction site in their neighbourhood — the materials, the workers, the equipment.

Class discusses the two questions from Textbook p. 144: Are all houses made of bricks? What other materials are used to build houses? Teacher records all materials students name on the board. Teacher then adds mud, stone, bamboo, wood, and metal sheets if not already mentioned.

Teacher explains how mud bricks are made — mixed, pressed into moulds, baked — drawing a parallel to how pottery clay is prepared. Students discuss: how is a brick like a pot? How is it different? Textbook p. 144 illustrations of different houses anchor the discussion.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks answering the question from Textbook p. 144: 'Why do you think mud houses are better for the environment?' Teacher prompts: think about what the material comes from and where it goes when the house is no longer used.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare building materials across different house types and explain why a particular material suits its context.
periods.section_context: Mud bricks, brick moulds, kiln firing of bricks; diverse house materials (brick, stone, mud, bamboo, wood); Rohan in Jaipur; mud house with cow-dung plaster.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether any elder in their family or community has lived in a house with a mud floor or mud wall. The cow-dung plaster tradition is a good opening — let students share what they know without framing it for them.

periods.activity_title: A World of Houses — Naming and Sorting
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Guessing the name of each type of house and filling in a table (p. 145)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of house types on p. 145 (tent, multi-storey building, stone house, houseboat)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 145 and look carefully at the pictures of different house types without writing yet. Teacher asks them to observe: what material is used, where might this house be found, who might live in it?

Students fill in the table in Textbook p. 145, guessing the name of each house type from the pictures. Teacher circulates and asks students to explain their reasoning — 'What tells you this is a tent and not a shed?'

Class compares answers. Teacher writes the four house types on the board — tent, multi-storey building, stone house, houseboat — and beside each writes the environment or need it fits: nomadic travel, dense city, rocky terrain, life on water. Students copy this into their notebooks.

Students look around at the houses in their neighbourhood and write one sentence answering the question from Textbook p. 144: 'What are the houses made of?' This grounds the global variety in their own local observation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify diverse types of houses from visual evidence and link each type to the material and environment it reflects.
periods.section_context: Tent, multi-storey building, stone house, houseboat; house materials observed in the student's own neighbourhood.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students have moved from another region, invite them to describe a house type they have seen there. The table on p. 145 is a scaffold — the reasoning behind each answer matters more than the label.

periods.activity_title: Make a Wall — Testing Brick Arrangements
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Making bricks with a mould and testing two stacking arrangements for sturdiness (p. 146)
materials: Matchboxes (outer sleeve only) or small paper boxes as moulds
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram of two brick-stacking arrangements on p. 146

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 146 and look at the two brick-stacking diagrams. Teacher asks: 'Before we test, which arrangement do you think will be sturdier — and why?' Students make a brief prediction in their notebooks.

Working in pairs, students press clay or dough into matchbox moulds to form six to eight small bricks. They allow the bricks a short rest on newspaper while the teacher briefly demonstrates the two arrangements from Textbook p. 146 on the board.

Pairs build the same number of bricks into each arrangement and gently push each wall from the side. They observe and record: which falls more easily, which stays standing. Teacher asks pairs to explain what they see.

Class compares findings. Teacher connects the interlocking arrangement to real brick walls students may have seen during construction. Students note their conclusion in one sentence: 'The ___ arrangement was sturdier because ___'.

periods.implied_lo: Students can test two structural arrangements of the same material and use their observations to explain which arrangement is stronger and why.
periods.section_context: Clay or dough bricks; matchbox mould; two stacking arrangements (aligned versus staggered/interlocking); sturdiness test by pushing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let students predict before they test and revisit their prediction after. Ask: 'Did what you see surprise you? Why do you think builders use the sturdier arrangement for real walls?'

periods.activity_title: Safety Rules — At the Site and at Home
periods.textbook_anchor: Brick by Brick — Discussion on safety rules at home and at school (p. 146)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of construction site safety gear on p. 146

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the construction-site illustration in Textbook p. 146 and asks students to identify the safety gear worn by workers. Students name helmets, boots, and any other items they can see. Teacher asks: 'Why do you think each piece of gear exists?'

Class discusses the two questions from Textbook p. 146: Are there safety rules at home? Do we have safety rules at school? Teacher records student responses in two columns on the board. Students share rules they know — not climbing on furniture, washing hands, walking (not running) on stairs.

Students choose one safety rule that matters most to them — at home, at school, or at a construction site — and write it on a strip of paper, then illustrate it with a small drawing. Strips are collected and read aloud by the teacher as a class 'safety charter'.

Teacher closes with a reflection question: 'A construction worker wears a helmet even on a day when nothing seems likely to fall — why is that a good habit?' Students share briefly, arriving at the idea that safety rules work by being followed always, not only when danger is visible.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why safety rules exist in working and living environments and practise articulating a personal safety commitment.
periods.section_context: Construction site safety gear (helmet, boots); safety rules at home; safety rules at school; worker safety practices.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After students name school safety rules, ask who decided those rules and whether they think every rule is fair. The goal is reflection, not rote recitation — students should be able to say why a rule exists.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Pot-Making and Artistic Inspiration
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Writing about the process of pot-making and how artists get ideas (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the first two writing prompts from Textbook p. 147 aloud: 'What is the process of pot-making?' and 'How do artists get ideas for their arts?' Class discusses both questions orally before writing. Students recall the steps from their earlier clay work and the patterns unit.

Students write their responses to both prompts in their notebooks, drawing on what they have discussed. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck: 'Think about what Appooppan did first — what did he need before he could start?'

Students share their answers in pairs, then two or three volunteers share with the class. Teacher notes on the board any steps or ideas students have named for artistic inspiration — nature, observation, tradition — and asks: 'Where else might an artist look for ideas beyond plants and animals?'
Teacher closes with the third prompt from Textbook p. 147 as an oral warm-up: 'What is a kiln?' Students give a brief oral definition, consolidating understanding of the firing process.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a multi-step craft process in sequence and articulate where artistic ideas come from, drawing on observation of the natural world.
periods.section_context: Pot-making process (collect clay, knead, shape, decorate, fire in kiln); artists' inspiration from nature (plants, animals, patterns); definition of kiln.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether they have ever drawn something because they noticed it in nature — a leaf, a bird, a cloud. This bridges their own experience to the idea of artistic inspiration without stating it as a rule.

periods.activity_title: What Are Houses Made Of? — Writing and Reasoning
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Writing about what houses are made of and why different kinds of houses exist (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the writing prompt from Textbook p. 147 — 'What are houses made of?' — and the discussion prompt 'Why do we have different kinds of houses?' Class discusses both orally first. Students contribute materials and reasons from their earlier observation of local houses and the house-types table.

Students write a response to the prompt 'What are houses made of?' in their notebooks, listing at least three materials and giving one reason each material is used. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Why is stone good in some places but not others?'

Class discusses 'Why do we have different kinds of houses?' Teacher steers toward geography, climate, materials available, and family size as reasons. Students add one more sentence to their written answer explaining why people in different places choose different materials.
Students draw three different kinds of houses in their notebooks as directed by Textbook p. 147, labelling each with its material and one place where it is commonly found.

periods.implied_lo: Students can give reasoned explanations for why housing materials and forms vary across environments and needs.
periods.section_context: Houses made of brick, stone, mud, bamboo, wood; reasons for diverse housing (climate, geography, available materials, family needs); three drawn house types.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students raise the idea of cost or poverty in relation to housing type, treat it respectfully and extend it: ask what makes one material more available than another in a given place. Avoid framing simpler houses as inferior.

periods.activity_title: What Would Happen Without Patterns? — A Thinking Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Discussion on what would happen if there were no patterns in nature (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 147: 'What would happen if there were no patterns in nature?' Students first think quietly for a moment, then share initial ideas. Teacher records the most interesting responses on the board without evaluating them.

Class explores the question in small groups. Each group picks one animal that has a pattern (zebra, leopard, squirrel, peacock) and discusses: would that animal survive differently without its pattern? Why? Groups share their reasoning with the class.

Teacher broadens the discussion: if plants had no repeating leaf or flower patterns, how would artists who find inspiration in nature be affected? Students connect the question to Mini's decoration work and the pottery-pattern tradition from earlier in the chapter.

Teacher closes with the safety-gear discussion prompt from Textbook p. 147 as a brief exit: 'Why do people wear helmets at construction sites?' Students give a quick oral answer, reinforcing the safety theme alongside the patterns reflection.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct reasoned predictions about what would change in the natural and human world if a natural phenomenon were absent.
periods.section_context: Patterns on animals (zebra, leopard, squirrel, peacock) and their functions; patterns as inspiration for artists; construction site helmets and their purpose.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This is a predictive reasoning discussion — there is no single right answer. Encourage students to build on one another's ideas rather than simply giving their own. Ask: 'Does anyone want to add to what was just said, or respectfully disagree?'

periods.activity_title: How Are Everyday Things Made? — An Elder Interview
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Finding out how common objects like pencils, erasers, pens, and notebooks are made by asking elders (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the inquiry prompt from Textbook p. 147: 'Find out how some commonly used objects like pencils, erasers, pens, and notebooks are made — ask your elders.' Since this activity is brought into the classroom sitting, teacher asks students what they already know or can guess about how one of these objects is made.

Students pick one object — pencil, eraser, pen, or notebook — and write down all the steps they think are involved in making it, in order, based on their own reasoning. They may draw simple diagrams beside each step.

Small groups share and compare their guessed sequences for different objects. Teacher facilitates: 'What raw material does a pencil start as? What does it need to become before it can be used?' Groups refine their steps through discussion, applying the idea of a multi-step making process the chapter has built.

Each group presents their sequence orally — one member speaks a step, the next continues, until the process is complete. Teacher closes by connecting all four sections of the chapter: clay is shaped into pots, clay is shaped into bricks, patterns in nature inspire decoration, and everyday objects are also shaped through a deliberate making process. Students write one sentence: 'All made things start with ___'.

periods.implied_lo: Students can reason through the steps of an unfamiliar making process using what they know about materials, tools, and sequence, and present their thinking clearly.
periods.section_context: Pencil, eraser, pen, notebook as everyday made objects; reasoning about raw materials and making steps; connecting all chapter sections through the theme of 'making'.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After groups present, ask: 'Did talking with others change what you thought the steps were?' This surfaces collaborative inquiry as a way of knowing. If a student mentions something an elder at home told them, elevate that knowledge alongside the group's reasoning.

assessment_items.question_text: Mini's grandfather Appooppan makes pots from clay. Which of the following best describes why pottery-making knowledge is described as 'passed within a family'?

options.label: A
options.text: Younger family members watch, help, and learn the craft from older family members who already know it.

options.label: B
options.text: Clay pots can only be made by people who belong to a potter's family, so the skill cannot be learned by others.

options.label: C
options.text: Schools teach pottery-making to every child, so all families end up knowing the craft.

options.label: D
options.text: Potters write down all their steps in a book so that anyone can read and repeat them.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests recognition of intergenerational craft transmission as described in the section narrative about Mini, Ammu, and Appooppan.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a traditional craft serves everyday needs and is passed within a community.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses hereditary community practice with biological exclusivity — they have not understood that craft knowledge is social and learnable, not genetically restricted.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has not engaged with the section's specific content about family-based transmission and has substituted a familiar schooling context instead.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student understands that knowledge can be recorded but misses the chapter's explicit framing of oral and hands-on transmission within the family.

assessment_items.question_text: When making clay from soil, you must sieve the soil, add water, and knead it. Why is each of these three steps needed before you can shape an object?
expected_elements: Sieving removes pebbles, leaves, and plant parts so the clay is smooth and will not crack or crumble unevenly.
Adding water makes the dry soil particles stick together so the mixture can be shaped.
Kneading works the water evenly into the soil to make a dough that holds its form when pressed.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete answer names all three steps and gives a reason for each. Award partial credit for two steps with reasons. The activity was carried out with locally sourced soil, so references to 'school compound soil' or 'damp soil from home' are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step material preparation process and explain how each step changes the material's properties.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

Adding water makes the dry soil particles stick together so the mixture can be shaped.
Kneading works the water evenly into the soil to make a dough that holds its form when pressed.

assessment_items.task: Draw two potter's products that a family like Mini's might make. On each product, draw a pattern that could decorate it. Beside your drawing, write one sentence saying what the object is used for.
assessment_items.scaffold: Choose two objects from: pot, gullak, kulhad, birdbath, or any other clay item you know. Draw each object and add a pattern — the pattern can be lines, dots, shapes, or anything you like. Write one sentence for each: 'This ___ is used for ___.'
format_of_output: Two labelled drawings of potter's products, each decorated with a pattern
One sentence per drawing stating the object's use
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any recognisable clay object. Patterns need not be elaborate — any deliberate repeating element counts. The use-sentence should reflect genuine everyday function, not a copied phrase.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of craft objects and their uses through drawing and oral explanation.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Student can represent craft objects accurately enough to be recognisable and communicate their function, showing that drawing is a valid mode of presenting knowledge.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold names four objects to reduce blank-page anxiety; students who draw a different clay item they know should receive full credit — the scaffold is a prompt, not a limit.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response shows two distinct objects, each with a visible repeating pattern element and a use-sentence that makes functional sense (e.g. 'This kulhad is used for drinking tea'). A weak response draws two similar or unlabelled blobs with no pattern or with a sentence that only restates the object name.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot yet write the sentence in full may dictate it to the teacher or draw a small scene showing the object in use — both demonstrate the same implied_lo.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the primary mode Mini uses in the section; combining it with a written use-sentence connects the craft tradition to its social function.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these six images showing steps in making a pot. Which step comes FIRST in the correct order?

options.label: A
options.text: Shaping the clay on the spinning wheel.

options.label: B
options.text: Collecting clay from a wet or muddy place.

options.label: C
options.text: Baking the shaped pot in the kiln.

options.label: D
options.text: Decorating the dry pot with colours.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students can identify the starting point of the production sequence from the Textbook p. 139 image set.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sequence the steps of a production process by reading visual evidence and explaining their reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has identified a central, memorable step (wheel-throwing) and placed it first — they know it is important but have not reasoned through what must happen before shaping is possible.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be working backwards from the finished product (the baked pot) and conflating the last visible transformation with the first step.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has confused the final finishing step with the starting point, suggesting they have not internalised the raw-material-to-finished-product direction of the sequence.

assessment_items.question_text: You have been asked to draw the pattern on a neem leaf. Describe in two or three sentences what you would observe on the leaf before drawing it.
expected_elements: Names a visible repeating element on the leaf (veins, leaf-edge shape, arrangement of smaller leaflets on the stem).
Describes the repeating quality — for example, that the same vein shape appears on both sides, or that leaflets are arranged in pairs.
Mentions that observation before drawing helps get the pattern accurate or shows what repeats.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate observation of a neem leaf or a locally familiar leaf. Students who describe a different plant's leaf pattern rather than neem are demonstrating the same skill — accept with full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe, draw, and describe repeating patterns found on plants in their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

expected_elements: Names a visible repeating element on the leaf (veins, leaf-edge shape, arrangement of smaller leaflets on the stem).
Describes the repeating quality — for example, that the same vein shape appears on both sides, or that leaflets are arranged in pairs.
Mentions that observation before drawing helps get the pattern accurate or shows what repeats.

assessment_items.task: Draw one animal that has a pattern on its body. Then draw one object from your home or school that also has a pattern. Write one sentence connecting the two: how is the animal's pattern similar to the pattern on the object?
assessment_items.scaffold: Animal patterns you could draw: zebra stripes, leopard spots, squirrel stripes, peacock feathers. Object patterns you could draw: a checked cloth, tiled floor, woven mat, printed bag. Connection sentence starter: 'The ___ pattern on the ___ is similar to the ___ pattern on the ___ because both ___.'
format_of_output: One sentence connecting the two patterns
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any patterned animal, including local species not listed in the scaffold. The connection sentence is the key assessment point — it should name a shared quality (both repeat, both have the same shape, both cover a surface). Regional variation note: students in different parts of India may draw locally familiar patterned animals (peacock, monitor lizard, tiger) or local craft objects (kantha cloth, ajrakh fabric) — all are correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify, draw, and name repeating patterns on animals and everyday objects, connecting natural patterns to human artistic practice.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Student can observe patterns in both the natural and made world and articulate a connection between them — the core insight that artists draw from nature.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold lists familiar examples; a student who draws a different animal or a different object from their environment demonstrates the same skill and should receive full credit.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response shows two recognisably distinct patterns, correctly categorised (one animal, one object), with a connection sentence that names a shared structural quality (repetition, shape, coverage). A weak response draws two random images with no visible pattern or a connection sentence that only names colour similarity.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write the connection sentence may draw a shared-pattern element linking both drawings — an arrow or a zoomed-in matching section — as an equivalent demonstration.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Two drawings with a written connection sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing two subjects and then writing a comparative sentence mirrors the C&E activity and the chapter's nature-to-craft argument simultaneously.

assessment_items.question_text: Bricks and pots are both made from clay. Write two sentences: one explaining how making a brick is similar to making a pot, and one explaining one difference between them.
expected_elements: Similarity: both start with clay that is shaped and then baked in a kiln to make it hard and durable.
Difference: pots are shaped by hand or on a spinning wheel into a hollow vessel, while bricks are shaped by pressing clay into a rectangular mould.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any valid similarity (raw material, kiln firing) and any valid difference (shape, mould versus wheel, use). The item does not require both specific points above — any one accurate similarity and one accurate difference earns full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare building materials across different house types and explain why a particular material suits its context.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Similarity: both start with clay that is shaped and then baked in a kiln to make it hard and durable.
Difference: pots are shaped by hand or on a spinning wheel into a hollow vessel, while bricks are shaped by pressing clay into a rectangular mould.

assessment_items.question_text: Rohan sees four different houses: a tent, a multi-storey building, a stone house, and a houseboat. Which house would be MOST suited for someone who moves from place to place and needs shelter that can be packed and carried?

options.label: A
options.text: A multi-storey building, because it is the tallest and most visible from a distance.

options.label: B
options.text: A stone house, because stone is the strongest material available.

options.label: C
options.text: A tent, because it can be set up, packed away, and carried to a new location easily.

options.label: D
options.text: A houseboat, because water is found everywhere.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The item tests whether students can link a specific shelter need (mobility) to the most appropriate house type from the Textbook p. 145 set.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify diverse types of houses from visual evidence and link each type to the material and environment it reflects.

competency.competency_text: Identifies the needs of people in different situations – in terms of access to resources, equal opportunities, work distribution, and shelter

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has associated 'best' shelter with the most impressive or visible structure rather than with the specific need described — they have not applied the near-to-far reasoning of matching shelter to situation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has reasoned from material strength alone rather than from the need for portability — they know stone is durable but have not considered that durability and mobility are separate requirements.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has made an overgeneralisation ('water is everywhere'), showing they recognise the houseboat's water connection but have not thought through whether water is actually available in every location a traveller might go.

assessment_items.question_text: When you stacked bricks in two arrangements — one with all joints lined up and one with the joints staggered — one arrangement was sturdier. Which arrangement was sturdier, and why do you think staggering the joints makes a wall stronger?
expected_elements: Names the staggered (interlocking) arrangement as the sturdier one.
Explains that when joints are staggered, each brick overlaps the gap in the row below, so a push cannot travel straight through one crack all the way down the wall.
May note that real brick walls are built the same way for the same reason.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any explanation that captures the idea of load distribution or interruption of a straight crack path. Students who describe their observation in sensory terms ('it didn't fall when I pushed it') should be prompted to explain why, but the observation alone earns partial credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can test two structural arrangements of the same material and use their observations to explain which arrangement is stronger and why.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Names the staggered (interlocking) arrangement as the sturdier one.
Explains that when joints are staggered, each brick overlaps the gap in the row below, so a push cannot travel straight through one crack all the way down the wall.
May note that real brick walls are built the same way for the same reason.

assessment_items.task: Write your own 'Safety Charter' for one place: your home, your school, or a construction site. List three safety rules for that place. For each rule, write one sentence explaining why that rule keeps people safe.
assessment_items.scaffold: My Safety Charter for: ___. Rule 1: ___ — This rule is important because ___. Rule 2: ___ — This rule is important because ___. Rule 3: ___ — This rule is important because ___.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any genuine safety rule for the chosen place. The reason sentence is the key assessment point — it should connect the rule to a specific harm it prevents. Regional variation note: safety rules and practices may differ by region and household — any locally valid rule with a coherent reason earns full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why safety rules exist in working and living environments and practise articulating a personal safety commitment.

competency.competency_text: Identifies the needs of people in different situations – in terms of access to resources, equal opportunities, work distribution, and shelter

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Student can move from naming a rule to explaining its protective purpose — demonstrating that safety knowledge is functional reasoning, not rote recitation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold's three-slot format is a minimum; students who list more than three rules should be credited for all. Students who change the place mid-charter should be asked to choose one, then re-read the chart.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response gives three distinct rules for one place, each with a reason that names a specific risk the rule addresses (e.g. 'We must not run on the stairs because we could fall and hurt someone below us'). A weak response lists rules without reasons, or gives reasons that restate the rule ('We must wear a helmet because helmets are for heads').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may draw the three rules as scenes and dictate the reason to the teacher — the reasoning is the assessment target, not the writing mechanics.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The charter format was introduced in the classroom activity, so students have a familiar scaffold; the written form makes the reasoning visible for teacher assessment.

assessment_items.question_text: Mini learned to decorate pots from her grandfather Appooppan. He learned from someone in his family before him. Why is it important that craft knowledge like pottery is shared from one generation to the next? Write three or four sentences.
look_for: Recognises that traditional craft knowledge (the skill of shaping, decorating, or firing clay) could be lost if not shared.
Connects craft knowledge to its usefulness in daily life — the objects potters make serve real needs (storing water, drinking tea, saving money).
Shows awareness that this kind of learning happens through watching, helping, and practising alongside an experienced person — not only from a book.
May extend the argument to cultural identity — the tradition carries a community's artistic style or local knowledge across time.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response should address at least two of the four look-for markers. Responses that draw on personal family experience or local craft tradition should be credited generously — the item is evaluative and personal examples strengthen the argument.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a multi-step craft process in sequence and articulate where artistic ideas come from, drawing on observation of the natural world.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

look_for: Recognises that traditional craft knowledge (the skill of shaping, decorating, or firing clay) could be lost if not shared.
Connects craft knowledge to its usefulness in daily life — the objects potters make serve real needs (storing water, drinking tea, saving money).
Shows awareness that this kind of learning happens through watching, helping, and practising alongside an experienced person — not only from a book.
May extend the argument to cultural identity — the tradition carries a community's artistic style or local knowledge across time.

assessment_items.question_text: People in different parts of India live in very different kinds of houses — tents, mud houses, stone houses, multi-storey buildings, houseboats. Give two reasons why people build different kinds of houses, and explain how each reason connects to the environment or needs of the people who live there.
look_for: First reason is clearly stated and connected to environment or need (e.g. geography — people near water build houseboats; rocky terrain — stone is the most available material).
Second reason is distinct from the first and also connected to a different environmental or social factor (e.g. climate — mud keeps homes cool in hot places; economic availability of materials).
Each reason is explained, not just named — the student says why the environmental factor leads to that house type.
May draw on personal knowledge of local houses or houses seen in the chapter to illustrate the reason.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: students will draw on their own region's housing materials and climate — answers referencing thatch, bamboo, lime plaster, or other regional materials are correct and should be credited. The explanatory link between reason and house type is the key assessment point.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can give reasoned explanations for why housing materials and forms vary across environments and needs.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: First reason is clearly stated and connected to environment or need (e.g. geography — people near water build houseboats; rocky terrain — stone is the most available material).
Second reason is distinct from the first and also connected to a different environmental or social factor (e.g. climate — mud keeps homes cool in hot places; economic availability of materials).
Each reason is explained, not just named — the student says why the environmental factor leads to that house type.

assessment_items.question_text: A leopard has spots on its body. Artists who decorate pots sometimes use a similar spot pattern. What does this tell us about where artists find ideas for their designs?

options.label: A
options.text: Artists copy each other's work from books and magazines to find new ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: Artists look at patterns in the natural world — on animals, plants, and other living things — and use them as inspiration.

options.label: C
options.text: Artists only use patterns that were invented by potters hundreds of years ago and have not changed since.

options.label: D
options.text: Artists use random shapes that have nothing to do with anything they have seen before.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests the chapter's central argument that natural patterns inspire human artistic practice, connecting the Patterns in Nature section to the Let us reflect discussion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct reasoned predictions about what would change in the natural and human world if a natural phenomenon were absent.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not engaged with the chapter's specific argument about nature as a source of inspiration and has defaulted to a generic idea of artists copying from other artists.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has partially understood the tradition angle (pottery patterns have a history) but has frozen the tradition — not recognising that artists continue to look at nature freshly rather than repeating old fixed forms.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has rejected any source of inspiration entirely, suggesting they have not made the connection between the natural patterns section and the craft/art sections of the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: Think about how a pencil is made. Starting with the raw material (wood and graphite), write three steps that you think happen before a pencil is ready to use.
expected_elements: Identifies a raw material for the pencil casing (wood) and for the writing core (graphite or a dark material).
Describes at least one shaping step — cutting, sawing, pressing, or forming the wood into a pencil shape.
Describes a joining or finishing step — putting the graphite inside, sharpening the tip, or adding paint or a label.
assessment_items.annotation: This is a reasoning task, not a recall task — there is no single correct sequence. Award credit for any logical, sequential response that starts with raw material and ends with something usable. Students who reason from what they know about wood or graphite without having been explicitly taught pencil manufacturing are demonstrating the target skill.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can reason through the steps of an unfamiliar making process using what they know about materials, tools, and sequence, and present their thinking clearly.

Describes at least one shaping step — cutting, sawing, pressing, or forming the wood into a pencil shape.
